title: Constellation Bid
protagonist: Aisha Odom, constellation architect at Solara Orbital, a small-satellite operator
primary_metric: satellites correctly placed in their target orbital plane per dollar of total launch cost

options.A: Consolidated Launch -- all 60 satellites on one large rocket into a single seed plane, then each off-plane satellite walks itself to its assigned plane on its own propellant
options.B: Distributed Launch -- six dedicated smaller rockets, one per target plane, so every satellite is delivered already correctly placed

scenario_constructions: Aisha Odom, Solara Orbital, and the specific 60-satellite constellation are fictional, invented for this case -- consistent with the corpus convention used for e.g. Priya Nakamura / Meridian Orbital / Aurora-7 in The Conjunction Call.

The board vote / launch-slot-deposit deadline (Overview) is scenario texture with no real citable source, consistent with the Overview's mid-crisis framing, disclosed as a stated scenario detail rather than sourced externally.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Grounded in the real altitude the FCC approved for SpaceX's first operational Starlink shell (S1) -- a real, representative modern LEO small-satellite constellation altitude, since Solara itself is fictional and has no real filing.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Altitude sets orbital speed, which scales every delta-v in Challenge D3 directly (higher altitude, lower speed, cheaper plane changes, and vice versa).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Modeling a RAAN (orbital plane) change using the single-burn combined plane-change formula
modeling_assumptions.basis: The real, standard formula for a single-burn plane rotation at constant altitude/speed (S2). Real RAAN changes are normally achieved via slow J2-perturbation drift over weeks or months, not one large burn -- this case adopts the standard single-burn formula as its own stated, disclosed simplification, since the slow-drift model has no simple angle-to-cost relationship and would not exercise unit-circle trigonometry.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not change which angle is cheaper or more expensive (sin(delta-theta/2) still grows monotonically with the angle under either model), but does change the exact propellant figures in Challenge D3 and therefore which of the six groups clear the propellant allowance.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Consistent with the mass class the BIT-3 thruster is flight-qualified for -- the manufacturer's own published reference platform is a 14 kg 6U CubeSat (S3); Solara's satellite is stated as a slightly heavier bus to accommodate MA4's propellant allowance.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Every propellant figure in Challenge D3 scales directly and linearly with this value.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Per-satellite propellant allowance reserved for the post-launch plane-change walk
modeling_assumptions.basis: Not publicly reported for any real satellite (Solara is fictional); set as the case's own stated engineering-budget scenario, deliberately aggressive (about 27% of wet mass) so the walk is feasible for at least the smallest required angle, testing whether it remains feasible for larger ones.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the single most dilemma-relevant assumption in the case -- it is the exact line Challenge D3's feasibility check is measured against, and Option A's correctly-placed count (and therefore its whole primary metric) is directly sensitive to it.

balance.argument_a: The Consolidated Launch wins on the case's own computed primary metric: 10 satellites correctly placed for $6.3 million (1.587e-6 satellites/dollar) versus the Distributed Launch's 60 satellites for $45 million (1.333e-6 satellites/dollar) -- a 19.05% edge for Option A. Even though only the seed-plane group's satellites can actually complete their walk within the stated propellant allowance, the Consolidated Launch's rideshare cost is so much lower per kilogram that its per-dollar coverage still edges out the Distributed Launch's guaranteed-but-expensive full deployment.
balance.argument_b: The Distributed Launch is the only option that actually finishes the mission: every one of the sixty satellites is delivered correctly placed, with zero risk that a plane-change burn falls short of its propellant allowance. Option A's razor-thin 19.05% per-dollar edge depends on treating 50 stranded, wrongly-placed satellites as an acceptable trade for a lower headline launch bill -- a constellation architect answering only to a coverage map, not a spreadsheet, would call a five-sixths-incomplete constellation a failed mission regardless of what the per-dollar ratio says.
balance.margin_basis: Satellites correctly placed / total launch cost. Option A: 10 / $6,300,000 = 1.5873e-6 sats/$ (only the 10 seed-plane satellites clear Appendix D's 4.0 kg propellant allowance; all other groups require more propellant than allowed, per Challenge D3's feasibility check). Option B: 60 / $45,000,000 = 1.3333e-6 sats/$ (all six dedicated Electron launches deliver their ten satellites already correctly placed). margin_pct = (1.5873e-6 - 1.3333e-6) / 1.3333e-6 * 100 = 19.05%. Full arithmetic in RESEARCH_LOG.md and sensitivity_model.py.
balance.twist_effect: SpaceX's next rideshare price step (grounded in the real, repeated historical pattern S4 documents: $5,500/kg in 2019, $6,500/kg in 2023, $7,000/kg in 2026) is disclosed mid-discussion as a hypothetical near-term jump to $9,000/kg. Recomputed: Option A's total cost rises to $8,000,000, its ratio falls to 1.25e-6 sats/$ -- now BELOW Option B's unchanged 1.3333e-6 sats/$. The winner flips to B, by a 6.67% margin. The exact breakeven rideshare price is $8,411.76/kg -- verified by sensitivity_model.py's evaluate_twist().

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: wet_mass_kg (MA3, 15.0 kg) is a good-faith scenario estimate consistent with the BIT-3 thruster's real published reference-platform mass class (S3, a 14 kg 6U CubeSat) -- no real published mass exists for the fictional Solara constellation. sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep (run 2026-09-18) confirms this is the single most load-bearing assumption in the case: at +50% (22.5 kg) the correctly-placed count stays at 10, but Option A's total launch cost rises (heavier satellites cost more to launch), dropping its ratio to 1.058e-6 sats/$ -- BELOW Option B's 1.333e-6, flipping the winner to B at a 26.0% margin, a genuine SPEC-cap breach in the opposite direction. At -50% (7.5 kg) every group's propellant requirement halves, so the 60-degree groups (20 satellites) newly clear the 4.0 kg allowance, raising the correctly-placed count to 30 and Option A's ratio to 9.524e-6 sats/$, a 614% margin -- also a cap breach, this time widening Option A's win far past defensible. This is disclosed in full, not eliminated by retuning: 15.0 kg is itself the case's honest best-effort estimate grounded in a real reference mass class, not an arbitrary dial, and it is the single figure a Hero should press hardest on.

propellant_allowance_kg (MA4, 4.0 kg) is a good-faith scenario estimate for a fictional constellation's engineering budget -- no public per-satellite figure exists for any real constellation, since operators do not publish this. sensitivity_model.py's mechanical +/-50% sweep confirms real, asymmetric fragility: at -50% (2.0 kg) the correctly-placed count and the margin are unchanged from the base case (19.05%, A wins) -- even the smallest nonzero walk (5.399 kg required at 60 degrees) already fails at the base 4.0 kg allowance, so a stricter allowance changes nothing further. At +50% (6.0 kg) the 60-degree groups (20 satellites) newly clear the allowance, raising the correctly-placed count to 30 and pushing Option A's margin to 257%, a real cap breach. This is disclosed in full -- MA4 is the assumption most likely to move the case if it turns out to be wrong in the generous direction, and a Hero who challenges this specific figure is raising exactly the right question.

altitude_km (MA1, 550 km) is a good-faith scenario estimate grounded in a real precedent (S1, SpaceX's first Starlink shell) -- no real altitude filing exists for the fictional Solara constellation. sensitivity_model.py's +/-50% sweep (275 km and 825 km) found NO change in the correctly-placed count or the margin in either direction -- across that whole range the feasibility pattern (only the 0-degree group clears the propellant allowance) does not cross a threshold, so the base case's 19.05% margin is, perhaps counter-intuitively, genuinely robust to this particular assumption. Disclosed here for completeness -- this is the one FLEX[] parameter that does NOT destabilize the verdict, a real and worth-naming finding in its own right, not just a formality.

facilitator.twist: SpaceX's next rideshare price step is disclosed mid-discussion: following the real, repeated historical pattern of roughly $500-$1,000/kg increases (2019: $5,500/kg; 2023: $6,500/kg; 2026: $7,000/kg -- Appendix H, S4), a hypothetical next jump to $9,000/kg is announced as the price Solara's launch would actually be booked at.
